about_this_file: printfix13: print-only wording for the print series (tools/book/series_text.py). 'about' is the one-page 'About this book, and how to use it' at the front of each book. 'ledes' replace a chapter's opening line in print. 'swaps' are exact find/replace pairs on a chapter's printed HTML (each must match exactly once, or build_series.py stops); {page:KEY} becomes a page slot in this book and {ref:SLUG} the series name of a chapter. The online pages are not changed by anything here.

1.what: This book starts with you. It looks at where your way of seeing things came from, how you are wired today, how feelings work, why your worth was never a score, how personality works and how minds can work differently.
1.who: It is for anyone who wants to understand themselves a little better, at their own pace. You don’t need a partner, a problem or a diagnosis to read it, and nothing in it is a test.

2.what: This book is for the heavy days. It covers stress, sleep and rest, anger, worry, low mood and trauma, grief, repair after hurt, the slow work of change, and what matters to you.
2.who: It is for anyone going through a hard stretch, and for anyone standing beside someone who is.

3.what: This book is about the people around you. It looks at how pace and tone pull people out of step, how words land, why two people remember the same moment differently, belonging and trust, love in its many forms, the pull of groups, and how to help someone without burning out.
3.who: It is for partners, families, friends, roommates and teams, and for anyone who has wondered why a kind conversation went wrong.

4.what: This book is about the work of sharing a life: the jobs nobody sees, a simple check of whether the way you share them can last, how much of a reaction is leftover stress, two kinds of fair, and a gentle monthly look back.
4.who: It is for anyone who shares a home, a family or a job, whether that is a couple, a family, roommates, co-parents or coworkers. Most of it also works if you are the only one reading.

about.how: Read the chapters in any order. Each holds the core of a chapter. The expanded version of every chapter, with more research, more examples and more to try, is free to read online. The code at the end of each chapter opens it on your phone.

about.ideas_lead: Five ideas run under the whole series.
ideas: Count the unseen work too, the noticing, remembering and planning, yours and other people’s.
Fix the setup, not the person
When something keeps going wrong, change the arrangement around it before you blame anyone.
How full your day already is changes how every word sounds, so check yourself before you react.
Tune how you send and receive
People differ in pace, tone and wiring, and a mismatch is something to translate, never a fault.
Jobs nobody owns drift to whoever notices first, and a named owner and a real thank-you stop the drift.
about.program: Some chapters mention the six-week program, a free plan on the website with one small step a week (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01). The workbook has a planner for it.

ledes.preface: Running a shared life takes a lot of work that nobody sees. This opening chapter helps you make that work visible, to yourself and to anyone you share it with, so that you can talk about it fairly and kindly.
ledes.afterword: A short look back over the whole series: what each book in the series was for, the few ideas that run through all of them, and where to go next.

titles.afterword: What the series adds up to

faq_lede: Some questions this book tends to raise, with short answers and where to read more.

1: Do I need to remember my childhood clearly for the first chapter to help?

Most people remember a handful of scenes and a general feeling, and that is plenty. The first chapter asks about the rules your home ran on, such as how feelings were handled or who did the worrying. Those rules tend to show up in how you react today more than in any one memory, so start with one rule you can name. Where your lens came from walks you through it.
What if looking back brings up something painful?
Stop there, and come back another day if you want to. Nobody has to finish a page.
I think I might be autistic or have ADHD. Can this book tell me?

It can’t, and nothing in it is a test. Minds that work differently describes how some minds work, so that you might recognize yourself or someone you love, and it says who can talk you through an assessment if you want one. Plenty of people find the descriptions useful whether or not they ever look for a diagnosis.
Can a grown-up really change their personality?

A little, slowly, and mostly by practicing the thing you want to be more like. Personality, temperament and change treats traits as sliders that move a few notches over the years. Every setting has its gifts and its costs, so the aim is a better fit with your life more than a new you.
My partner isn’t interested in any of this. Is it still worth reading?

Yes. This book is about you, and it works if you are the only person in your home who ever opens it. Knowing your own wiring and weather makes it easier to say what you need, and the people around you often notice the change before they notice the book. If you later want to look at things together, Book 3 and Book 4 are written for that.
2: I lost my temper and said something I regret. Is it too late to put it right?

It rarely is. A short apology that names what you did, without a “but,” and a plan for next time go a long way, even days later. Healing after hurt shows how a repair goes, and Anger has a pause plan for the next time the heat rises.
Someone I love is grieving. What should I say?

Something simple and true, such as “I don’t know what to say, but I’m here.” Saying the name of the person who died is usually a kindness. Practical help, like a meal, a ride or a walk, often means more than the right words, and so does still being there a few months on. Loss, grief and big life changes has more.
I keep starting good habits and dropping them. What am I doing wrong?

Probably nothing, except starting too big. Habits stick when the first step is tiny, tied to something you already do and easy to restart after a missed day. Habits and change shows how to shrink a step until it takes two minutes or less.
Do I have to forgive someone who hurt me?

No. Forgiveness, trust and going back are all yours to choose, in your own time, and you can heal even if the other person never says sorry. Healing after hurt explains what forgiving means and what it doesn’t.
3: We care about each other but keep falling out. Where do we start?

Start with pace. Two people who both care can still run at different speeds, talk things through at different times and feel urgency about different things. Why we get out of tune helps you spot which one is catching you, and the workpaper Same moment, different speeds lets you compare your answers side by side.
Our messages keep going wrong. Any quick fixes?

Read a message twice before you reply, and assume the warmest tone that fits the words. Short texts lose their tone on the way, so a quick “Do you mean…?” saves a lot. How communication works covers this, and the Chat analyzer on the website lets you check how a message may land before you send it.
My family remember things completely differently from me. Who is right?

Often both of you, a little. Memory keeps what mattered to each person and quietly fills in the rest. How we see each other explains why, and suggests asking “What do you remember about that day?” before you share your own version.
How do I help someone without wearing myself out?

Ask what kind of help they want, do the part you can keep doing, and say plainly where your limit is. Help that lasts usually comes from more than one person. Helping others well has a part on noticing when you are running on empty.
I feel like I don’t quite belong anywhere. Is something wrong with me?

No. Feeling on the edge of a group is common, especially after a move, a breakup or a change of job. Belonging tends to grow from small, repeated contact with the same few people. Attachment, trust and belonging and Groups, influence and culture both have ideas to try.
4: My partner thinks the split is already fair. Where do we start?

With a week of facts. Fill in Who did what for one ordinary week, each of you writing only what you did yourself, and look at it together over a cup of tea. The planning and remembering often surprises both people. The work nobody sees explains why, and Is the split working? has a part for when only one of you wants to try.
There are three or more of us. Does any of this still work?

Yes. Roommates, families with older children and teams can all use the same pages. Compare each person’s share with an even share, which is 100 divided by the number of people, or with the split you agreed. “How the numbers work” at the back of this book (page {page:numbers}) shows the math.
One of us works much longer paid hours. Is it fair to count only housework?

It isn’t, and the book doesn’t. If you have agreed an uneven split at home because one of you works longer hours outside it, the setup score compares against that agreement instead of an even split. Two kinds of fair explains the difference between fair by results and fair by promises.
Can children have jobs with an owner too?

They can own jobs that suit their age, with an adult as the backstop who notices if it slips. Owning one small job from start to finish, such as feeding the cat or packing a school bag, is a good first step. Keep the planning and remembering with the adults until a child is ready for a piece of it, and say thank you out loud.
Talking about chores always turns into a fight. What can we do?

Pick a calm time, never the moment something has been left undone. Check how full each of your stress tanks is first, because a full tank makes every word land harder. Full tanks and different angles shows how, and The monthly look-back gives you a short, regular time to talk so that nothing has to wait for an argument.
Does this work at work, in a team?

Yes. The same quiet jobs exist at work, such as booking the room, chasing the late reply and noticing that the printer is out of paper, and a named owner and a real thank-you help there too. Most of the pages in this book work for a team with the word “home” swapped for “work.”

jobs.title: A list of jobs to start from
jobs.lede: Most homes share some of these. Check the ones that happen in yours, cross out the rest and add your own at the bottom. Then give each checked job one owner and, if you like, a backstop who notices if it slips, as in Is the split working?. The same list is in the Quick look tool on the website, under Who does what? Quick look, and the workpaper One owner per job has room for the names.

first_month.title: Your first month, week by week
first_month.lede: If you would like an order to follow, here is one. Each week takes a few minutes a day at most, and a missed week is fine. The six-week program on the website does the same at a gentler pace.
weeks: See the work. Each of you fills in Who did what for one ordinary week, writing only what you did yourself.
Give every job a name. Go through the job list on the next pages together and use One owner per job to agree an owner for each.
Check the tanks. Each of you fills in How much are you carrying? on two or three days, then work out the setup score with the setup calculator or on paper.
Look back together. Sit down for twenty minutes with What keeps coming back?, choose one small change, and put the next look-back in the diary.

3.title: Words for hard moments
3.lede: Some ways to say the hard parts, collected in one place. Change the words until they sound like you.
groups: “Is now a good time to talk about Saturday, or would tomorrow be better?”
“Something has been on my mind, and I’d rather tell you than let it grow.”
“I’d like to understand how it looked from your side.”
“When you said you were fine, did you mean it, or not really?”
“Can I check I’ve got this right?”
“I need twenty minutes. I’ll come back after that.”
“I’m not going anywhere. I just need some quiet.”
“That came out wrong. Can I try again?”
“I think we both meant well, and it still went sideways.”
“I’m sorry I was sharp with you earlier.”
“Do you want ideas, or would you like me to just listen?”
“I can do Tuesday evenings. Who else could we ask?”

4.title: Words for the talk
4.lede: Some ways to say the hard parts, collected in one place. Change the words until they sound like you.
groups: “Can we look at how the week went, together? I’d like us both to see it.”
“I’ve written down what I did this week. Would you do the same, so we can compare?”
“Is now a good time, or would after dinner be better?”
“I think a lot of the remembering lands on me. Can we talk about that?”
“I’m getting wound up. Can we stop for twenty minutes and come back at eight?”
“That came out sharper than I meant. Let me try again.”
“My tank is pretty full today, so I might sound angrier than I feel.”
“Could you own the trash from now on, from noticing it’s full to putting it out?”
“It’s yours now, so do it your way. I’ll only step in if you ask.”
“I’ll be the backstop this month. If it slips, I’ll mention it once, gently.”
“That’s a fair ask. I can’t take it on this week, but I could do Saturday’s grocery run instead.”
“I’m at my limit. Can we look at what else could drop?”
“Thanks for sorting the dentist. I noticed.”
“What’s one thing that felt easier this month?”
“Is anything from last week still sitting with you?”
